case_studies.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
case_studies.summary: GateWatch offers a very lightweight way to watch what large language models (LLMs) do by turning a few key features into simple Boolean rules. They built a system that keeps memory use down by 99.98% and adds almost no lag when running many probes on a model like Gemma‑2‑9B. The result is accurate monitoring that almost matches heavier methods while staying fast and tiny.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM deployments, add GateWatch to your monitoring stack: 1) Identify the key SAE features you need (about 4), 2) Deploy GateWatchServe to stream these binaries during inference, 3) Use the compact lookup tables to evaluate probes in parallel, keeping throughput above 97% and cache usage near 100%.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical monitoring tool for LLMs, directly impacting deployment, debugging, and compliance for infrastructure teams. It includes a released prototype (GateWatchServe) integrated with vLLM, indicating real-world readiness. While it offers immediate operational benefits, commercialization or service integration would require additional tooling, so monetisation potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
case_studies.summary: PIPETTE tackles prompt injection attacks on LLM agents by creating a purple‑team framework that pushes red‑team attacks to cover many strategies, then trains defenders with those attacks to build robust agents. It built a dictionary‑reward system for wider attack discovery and an on‑policy training pipeline that keeps normal tasks working while blocking injection. The result was agents with almost zero success for static attacks and strong resistance to adaptive attacks without losing performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLM services, use PIPETTE by: 1) integrating its dictionary‑reward red‑team to generate diverse injection scenarios, 2) feeding those scenarios into an on‑policy adversarial training loop for your models, 3) validating that attack success rates drop to near zero while task accuracy stays near baseline.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, a security concern relevant to IT infrastructure that could affect engineers managing LLM services. The approach includes an implementation and evaluation, indicating a usable system, but the work is still research‑grade with limited real‑world deployment evidence. Commercial use would require integration and testing in existing workflows, which could be done within a few months but is not immediately ready as a product.

case_studies.title: MaskPE: One Mask, Two Roles: Weight Placement and MAC Gating in Systolic Arrays
case_studies.abstract: Unstructured pruning reduces weight storage but does not inherently reduce execution cost in conventional weight-stationary systolic arrays. Packed nonzero weights must be restored to fixed processing-element positions, while zero-weight positions must preserve data forwarding. This paper presents MaskPE, a mask-directed systolic architecture that uses positional masks to steer nonzero weights during preload and clock-gate arithmetic registers in zero-weight processing elements during execution, reducing dynamic power while preserving systolic dataflow. At 50% sparsity, MaskPE reduces compressed weight storage by 34.9%, including metadata overhead. RTL validation confirms exact execution with no additional steady-state tile stalls, while gate-level simulations demonstrate 12.5--14.4% lower execution energy across samples of seven LLM projections.
case_studies.summary: MaskPE tackles the gap between weight pruning and energy savings in systolic arrays by routing non‑zero weights to processing elements and clock‑gating zero‑weights, cutting compressed weight storage by 34.9% and reducing execution energy by up to 14.4% at 50% sparsity.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a systolic‑array‑based inference engine, step 1: add a mask‑driven preload stage to send only non‑zero weights to the relevant PEs; step 2: enable clock‑gating on registers in PEs that receive zero‑weights; step 3: validate with RTL to ensure no stall or accuracy loss.
case_studies.relevance_tag: Hardware Optimization, Systolic Arrays, Sparse Computation
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on low-level hardware optimization for systolic arrays used in LLM acceleration. While it demonstrates energy savings and storage reduction, it does not provide a ready-to-deploy solution for IT engineers managing cloud or SaaS infrastructure. The implementation is still at RTL and simulation stages, lacking a production-ready system or API. Monetisation prospects for standard IT engineers are minimal within 90 days. Thus the overall relevance and immediate applicability are low.

case_studies.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
case_studies.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
case_studies.summary: This research shows that training vision models to be ready for direct weight edits by large language models can improve editing success, but it is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on a novel research method for training vision models to be more editable by LLMs. While it provides a benchmark and a new training technique (ERT), it is largely theoretical and experimental. The applicability to day‑to‑day IT infrastructure is minimal – no direct impact on SaaS tooling, endpoint management, SSO, or cloud services. The released code and framework provide some usable artifacts, but they target researchers rather than engineers needing immediate solutions. The monetisation potential is low; the method would require significant adaptation before it could be offered as a commercial service within 90 days. The overall signal is weak for our audience.

case_studies.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
case_studies.abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.
case_studies.summary: Sightline creates accurate data‑flow summaries for applications that call large language models, solving the problem of over‑tainting by showing which prompt placeholders actually influence LLM outputs. It uses a single forward pass and a small calibration set to prune over 40% of false flows while missing only about 1% of real ones. The result is a leaner, more precise flow analysis for LLM‑integrated code.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑integrated services, here is what to do: step 1, run a small calibration set to determine the acceptable miss rate α; step 2, integrate Sightline to analyse each model call and prune unnecessary taints; step 3, review the pruned flow reports to reduce false positives in your security checks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a niche research problem (data-flow summaries for LLM-integrated apps) with limited direct applicability to everyday IT engineering tasks like cloud, SSO, endpoint mgmt. The tool Sightline is experimental and not broadly usable yet. No clear commercial or quick deployment path. Hence low scores across all dimensions.
